definition: A regional or social variety of a language distinguished by pronunciation, grammar, or vocabulary.
etymology: From Greek 'dialektos' meaning 'discourse, way of speaking'
contextSentence: But what do the dialects spoken in dozens of countries around the world have in common?

definition: Developed gradually over time, especially from a simple to a more complex form.
etymology: From Latin 'evolvere' meaning 'to unroll, unfold'
contextSentence: English has evolved through generations of speakers.

definition: To find the origin or course of development of something.
etymology: From Old French 'tracier' meaning 'to follow, track'
contextSentence: We can trace the language from the present day back to its ancient roots.

definition: An instance of invading a country or region with an armed force.
etymology: From Latin 'invasionem' meaning 'an attack, invasion'
contextSentence: They started coming into the language with the Norman invasion of England in 1066.

definition: Overcame and took control of a place or people by military force.
etymology: From Old French 'conquerre', from Latin 'conquirere' meaning 'to seek out, procure'
contextSentence: When the French-speaking Normans conquered England.

definition: Exceptionally large or extensive.
etymology: From French 'massif', from Latin 'massa' meaning 'lump, mass'
contextSentence: Adding a massive amount of French and Latin vocabulary.

definition: The body of words used in a particular language or known to an individual.
etymology: From Medieval Latin 'vocabularium', from Latin 'vocabulum' meaning 'word, name'
contextSentence: Adding a massive amount of French and Latin vocabulary.

definition: Involving comparison between two or more things.
etymology: From Latin 'comparativus', from 'comparare' meaning 'to compare'
contextSentence: But comparative linguistics can help us by focusing on grammatical structure.

definition: The scientific study of language and its structure.
etymology: From Latin 'lingua' meaning 'language, tongue'
contextSentence: But comparative linguistics can help us by focusing on grammatical structure.

definition: Relating to grammar or conforming to the rules of grammar.
etymology: From Greek 'grammatikos' meaning 'of letters'
contextSentence: Comparative linguistics can help us by focusing on grammatical structure.

definition: According to a fixed plan or system; in a methodical way.
etymology: From Greek 'systematikos' meaning 'combined in a system'
contextSentence: German words starting with P systematically shifted to a PF sound.

definition: A person or thing that corresponds to or has the same function as another in a different context.
etymology: From 'counter' (opposite) + 'part'
contextSentence: While their Old English counterparts kept the P unchanged.

definition: Words adopted from one language into another.
etymology: From Old English 'borgian' meaning 'to lend, borrow'
contextSentence: Viking invaders added more borrowings from Old Norse into the mix.

definition: Originated or derived from an ancestor or earlier form.
etymology: From Latin 'descendere' meaning 'to come down, go down'
contextSentence: Just as the various Romance languages descended from Latin.

definition: A person or thing from which later forms developed; a forefather.
etymology: From Old French 'ancestre', from Latin 'antecessor' meaning 'predecessor'
contextSentence: Descended from their own common ancestor, known as Proto-Germanic.

definition: To build or form again; to re-create or re-establish based on available evidence.
etymology: From Latin 're-' (again) + 'construere' (to build)
contextSentence: We can only reconstruct it by comparing its descendants.

definition: The quality of being unchanging or achieving the same standard repeatedly.
etymology: From Latin 'consistentia' meaning 'standing firm'
contextSentence: Which is possible thanks to the consistency of the changes.

definition: Close similarities or connections between things; systematic relationships between sounds in related languages.
etymology: From Medieval Latin 'correspondentia', from 'correspondere' meaning 'to respond together'
contextSentence: We can find the same systematic similarities, or correspondences.

definition: Took the place of; forced something out of its position or role.
etymology: From Old French 'desplacer', meaning 'to move from a place'
contextSentence: And the Celtic languages it displaced in what is now Britain.

definition: Relating to the study of human history through excavation and analysis of physical remains.
etymology: From Greek 'arkhaios' (ancient) + 'logos' (study)
contextSentence: This is as far back as historical and archaeological evidence will allow us to go.

definition: In spite of that; however; all the same.
etymology: From 'never' + 'the' + 'less', Middle English compound
contextSentence: Are nevertheless speaking the same words shaped by 6,000 years of history.
